title: AI: Helping Students Join the Conversation
author: Rupert Wegerif
source: Expanding Dialogic Space with Rupert Wegerif (Substack)
summary: Rupert Wegerif, an education professor at Cambridge's Hughes Hall, uses the occasion of an Oracy Conference to argue that AI could serve as a powerful scaffold for helping students — particularly working-class students — develop the conversational fluency that genuine education requires. Opening with a reflection on why white working-class families in Grimsby told the BBC they wanted work preparation rather than 'education,' Wegerif argues the right response is not better marketing of school but making education genuinely dialogic: connected to real conversation, real communities, and real work. The article traces a vision in which AI becomes a conversational partner that allows students to practice academic dialogue without the social risks of failure in front of peers, lowering the floor for entry into genuine intellectual exchange. Wegerif is careful to distinguish between AI as a substitute for human dialogue (which it cannot replace) and AI as an equalizer that gives students who lack confident adult conversational models more exposure to reasoned back-and-forth. The piece connects to the broader oracy movement's claim that the most important gap in education is not knowledge but the capacity to participate meaningfully in spoken intellectual exchange.
points: The Grimsby mothers' preference for 'work' over 'education' is not anti-intellectual; it is a rational response to an education system that often fails to feel connected to the real world — and dialogic education is the most direct bridge between school and life.

AI's potential as an oracy scaffold is in providing low-stakes conversational practice: students who lack access to confident academic conversation models at home can practice the moves of reasoned dialogue with an AI before attempting them in front of peers.

Wegerif's distinction between AI as human-conversation substitute and AI as conversational equalizer is the article's most important claim: AI cannot replace the richness of human dialogue, but it can reduce the access gap for students whose home environments don't model academic discourse.

Cambridge's 'ivory tower' image is misleading, Wegerif argues — the university is deeply embedded in medicine, law, and public policy — and genuine education should model that same embeddedness in real communities rather than retreating into abstraction.

The oracy gap Wegerif identifies is structural, not individual: working-class students are not less intelligent or less capable of dialogue, but they have fewer opportunities to practice the specific conversational moves that academic and professional settings reward.
quotes: At the recent Oracy Conference here in my college at Cambridge, Hughes Hall, I found myself talking with Kate Paradine, CEO of Voice 21, about the new report, chaired by Estelle Morris, on why white working-class children are being left behind in education. Mothers in Grimsby interviewed by the BBC were saying that what mattered to them was not “education”, but work.

In my college I meet people working in medicine, law, architecture, engineering, business and public policy, most of them deeply engaged with hospitals, industry, government and communities. If even Cambridge, supposedly the peak of academia, is full of people connecting knowledge with practice, why does school still feel to so many families as if it is a detour from reality?

Why should this be reserved for adults already inside elite professional worlds? Imagine a mathematics lesson in which students run a market stall — pricing stock, working out wastage, and deciding whether to extend credit to a regular customer, while a rival stallholder undercuts them and the council warden threatens a fine.

The idea is to augment the existing knowledge-focused curriculum — perhaps accelerated with AI but with teachers guiding and framing throughout — and to show how that knowledge can be applied to understand real world situations and solve real world problems. Most of what human beings learn, we do not learn from books or formal lessons.

My own work on dialogic education has been inspired partly by Michael Oakeshott, who taught history for many years at Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge, and described education as joining “the conversation of mankind”. But we need to widen Oakeshott’s image beyond history, philosophy and classics.
We inherit long conversations: mathematics, science, history, literature, technology, craft, politics, religion and work. They are living traditions of argument, evidence, judgement and practice.
The third loop is deferred indefinitely: learn this now, you may need it later. AI-supported, multi-voiced cases could bring all three loops together.
